stops.name: Bow: Bryant & May, and White Slavery in London
stops.campa: Annie visits the match-workers of Bryant & May in Bow and hears how fourteen-hour days are paid a starvation wage further docked by fines for dropped matches or a trip to the lavatory, while phosphorus rots the girls' jaws. In her paper The Link she publishes White Slavery in London, naming the shareholders' profits against the workers' poverty. Two girls tell her plainly it is time someone came and helped; she resolves, unlike so many who wish a cause well, to risk something for it herself.
stops.quote: It is time some one came and helped us... Who will help? Plenty of people wish well to any good cause; but very few care to exert themselves to help it, and still fewer will risk anything in its support.
stops.quote_source: Annie Besant, An Autobiography (1893), recalling the match girls of 1888

stops.name: Bow, the Union of Women Match Makers, and the settlement
stops.campa: Bryant & May's management, enraged, tries to force the workforce to sign a denial and sacks those they suspect of talking to the press. Some fourteen hundred women and girls walk out. Annie raises strike funds, organises relief, and helps found the Union of Women Match Makers, one of the first unions of women workers in Britain. By the sixteenth of July the fines, the docked wages, and the phosphorus-tainted mess-room are abolished; the match girls have won, and unskilled women's unionism has its first great victory.

stops.name: Tower Hamlets, elected to the London School Board
stops.campa: On the strength of the match girls' victory and years on secularist and socialist platforms, Annie stands for the London School Board and tops the poll in Tower Hamlets with more than fifteen thousand votes, the largest of any candidate in England that year. Denied her own children by a court that called her unfit, she now sits in office over the education of London's poorest, free dinners, free boots, medical inspection, turning private grief into a public office she can actually wield.

stops.name: St James's Hall, the debate with Hyndman
stops.campa: Bradlaugh and the Marxist Henry Hyndman debate socialism versus individualism before a packed St James's Hall, and Annie, still Bradlaugh's ally on the secularist platform, watches the argument that will pull her toward socialism turn public and sharp. Within a year she will join the Fabian Society that Hyndman's rivals are founding, carrying into it the oratory she has spent a decade sharpening in halls just like this one, against opponents just as formidable.

stops.name: London, recruited to the Fabian Society by Shaw
stops.campa: George Bernard Shaw, twenty-eight and already certain of her gifts, recruits Annie into the young Fabian Society, calling it a triumph to have gained the woman he names the greatest orator in England. She lectures, writes, and organises for the Fabians as she once did for the secularists, and a friendship with Shaw takes root that will survive nearly every later change of her convictions, even the one that costs him her company as a fellow socialist.
stops.quote_source: George Bernard Shaw, on recruiting Besant to the Fabian Society, 1885

stops.name: London: Fabian Essays, and the lapsing socialist
stops.campa: Fabian Essays in Socialism appears at the end of 1889 with Annie's chapter, Industry Under Socialism, alongside Shaw's, Webb's, and Olivier's, twenty-seven thousand copies in two years, a landmark of English socialism. But by the time it is in the shops she has already met Blavatsky and joined the Theosophical Society; within a year she lets her Fabian membership lapse and breaks with the Marxists. Shaw and the others are stunned. She has changed convictions whole before, and will again.

stops.name: London, reviewing The Secret Doctrine for the Pall Mall Gazette
stops.campa: Asked to review Helena Blavatsky's vast, difficult Secret Doctrine for the Pall Mall Gazette, Annie sits with a book most reviewers would refuse outright and finds in it not nonsense but a rock, she writes, whence every faith's disjointed fragments were hewn. She will not simply endorse it and will not dismiss it either: all who keep an open door to truth, she concludes, will give scrutiny to any visitant, be the garb of Asia or of Europe. The door, once opened, does not close again.
stops.quote: All who keep an open door to Truth will give scrutiny to any visitant, be the garb of Asia or of Europe, be the tongue of Paris or of Ind.
stops.quote_source: Annie Besant, review of The Secret Doctrine, Pall Mall Gazette, 1889

stops.name: 17 Lansdowne Road, meeting Blavatsky
stops.campa: On the evening of the tenth of May, with her friend Herbert Burrows, Annie calls at 17 Lansdowne Road, Holland Park, where Helena Blavatsky keeps her London lodgings and the Blavatsky Lodge meets. The old Russian is exactly as strange as report has made her, and exactly as commanding. Before the evening ends Blavatsky has told Annie plainly that she wants her in the Society. Annie, freethinker of fifteen years, feels something in the room she has no vocabulary yet to name.

stops.name: 17 Lansdowne Road, joining the Theosophical Society
stops.campa: Eleven days after the meeting, Annie signs her name into the Theosophical Society. London's secularists and socialists alike are thunderstruck: the great materialist orator, kneeling, as they see it, to Asiatic mysticism and an old woman's cosmology of root-races and rounds. She will spend the rest of her life mapping the same clarity of purpose she brought to Bradlaugh's platform onto Blavatsky's cosmos, and will never again change her convictions this completely.

stops.name: Hall of Science, Why I Became a Theosophist
stops.campa: In the same Hall of Science where she first heard Bradlaugh fifteen years before, Annie now delivers the lecture Why I Became a Theosophist to the freethinkers who once claimed her as their own. She does not renounce the reasoning that carried her through secularism, birth control, and the picket line; she says only that Theosophy answers questions materialism left open. It is a fourth identity worn over the same restless hunger for a truth that will finally hold still.

stops.name: 19 Avenue Road, Blavatsky's deathbed: 'Keep the link unbroken'
stops.campa: Influenza scythes through London and takes Blavatsky at 19 Avenue Road on the eighth of May. Two nights before, she had charged the disciples at her side with the whole burden of the future: keep the link unbroken, do not let my last incarnation be a failure. Annie is among those at the bedside. Her body is burned at Woking; the ashes are divided between New York, London, and Adyar. Annie, forty-three and only two years a Theosophist, becomes overnight the movement's most capable voice.
stops.quote: Keep the link unbroken! Do not let my last incarnation be a failure.
stops.quote_source: H. P. Blavatsky, last message to the Esoteric School, recorded by those present, 6 May 1891

stops.name: Adyar, first landing in India
stops.campa: Four years a Theosophist, Annie sails for India for the first time to attend the Society's annual Convention at Adyar, the compound on the river outside Madras that Blavatsky and Olcott made the movement's world headquarters under its great banyan. She arrives already fluent in the doctrine and already loved by Indians who see in a white woman's reverence for their own philosophy something the Raj has rarely offered. Adyar, from this landing on, will be more truly her home than London ever was again.
